power_id text
1;2 Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026. Prospective participants received a study invitation link randomized to one of four conditions: access to BS-VT and prompted with reminder nudges, access to the BS-VT and prompted with goal-setting nudges, access to the BS-VT app alone, or given no access to the BS-VT app. These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2. Attrition led to a final sample size of 519 participants (M age = 4.33 years, SD age = 0.80, range = 2.97-6.00) who completed both baseline and endline surveys, see Figure 2. Attrition did not differ between groups (F(3, 808) = 1.23, p = .299). Note that higher SES predicted endline survey completion (β = 0.61, SE = 0.14, t = 4.35, p < .001). Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier. See Supplementary Methods for details about MoyaApp and recruitment process. A power analysis (β = 0.9) determined that a sample of 634 participants was necessary to detect a small effect (MDES f = 0.15). The final sample of 519 corresponds to a MDES of 0.166. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework Note. Participants who enrolled in the study (enrolled sample), completed both baseline and endline measures (final sample), accessed BS-VT, and engaged with BS-VT. Despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention (n = 30 engaged with BookSmart content).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05). Discussion
Here, we found that children from lower SES households and children with low baseline scores showed positive impacts in social-emotional, cognitive, and language skills when caregivers received behavioral nudges, albeit these effects were largely marginally significant (q < .1). Behavioral Nudges Increased Digital Parenting Tool Engagement and Child Outcomes
It’s also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings. Limitations and Future Directions

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 237 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p > .05 Insignificant values (p > .05) are blank.
p > .05 Insignificant values (p > .05) are left blank.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 65 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name setwd() calls found
Worldreader Analyses.R setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path))

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 12 distinct packages/libraries: car, corrplot, dplyr, emmeans, ggplot2, glmtoolbox, jtools, performance, pscl, qvalue, readxl, rstudioapi. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 216 columns across 3 data files.

Issues Identified

6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were randomized into four groups: BS-VT with goal-setting nudges, BS-VT with reminder nudges, BS-VT (no behavioral nudges), and a wait-listed control group.

Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026.

These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2.

Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier.

2 Participants were typically compensated 90 rand.

Four measurements are represented: (A) the number of times participants opened the BookSmart app, (B) the total amount of time participants spent in BookSmart, (C) the number of books participants completed in BookSmart, and (D) the number of Vroom Tips TM participants completed. .47 (0.04) < .001*** < .001*** 0.55 (0.04) < .001*** < .001*** 0.63 (0.04) < .001*** < .001*** Age 0.00 (0.00) .368 .692 0.00 (0.01) .764 .860 -0.01 (0.02) .467 .741 SES 0.06 (0.04) .159 .505 0.07 (0.19) .709 .842 0.07 (0.20) .733 .842 Observations 489 489 489 Multiple /Adjusted R² 0.22 / 0.21 0.29 / 0.28 0.35 / 0.34 Panel C Cognitive Skills Language Skills Academic Skills Treatment vs.

We recruited 20 caregivers through MoyaApp, as in study 1, and followed the same inclusion and exclusion criteria with the following addition: families were excluded from the study if the caregiver was not female and between the ages 18 to 45.

Most in-depth interview studies achieve saturation with samples of 9-17 (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022), suggesting that our sample size should have provided sufficient results. 7 participants were caregivers of 3 year olds, 5 were caregivers of 4 year olds, and 8 were caregivers of 5 year olds.

Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025.
