How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

This study is a mixed-methods impact evaluation of a digital parenting and shared book reading intervention (Worldreader's BookSmart app with embedded parenting tips, Vroom Tips TM ) on caregivers' self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and early childhood outcomes in South Africa. We further investigated whether behavioral nudges could promote sustained engagement. Study 1 consisted of a 4-arm randomized controlled trial (BookSmart, BookSmart with reminder nudges, BookSmart with goal-setting nudges, control group) where caregivers (N = 519) of children aged 3-5 years used BookSmart for 15 weeks. We found randomization to access the intervention (i.e., intent-to-treat) had no significant effect on caregiver or child outcomes. However, behavioral nudges, particularly goal-setting messages, increased caregiver engagement and improved cognitive and language skills specifically for disadvantaged children (i.e., children from lower-SES households and children with lower baseline skills). Greater intervention engagement (i.e., treatment-on-the-treated) was significantly associated with language skills and marginally associated with literacy skills. Study 2 consisted of qualitative interviews with caregivers (N = 20) before and after using BookSmart for 3 weeks. Results indicated that several barriers impacted caregivers' engagement with the intervention, including costs (e.g., airtime) and language accessibility (e.g., caregivers reported translating English books into their native language). Our results highlight that digital reading interventions have the potential to support early childhood development, while stressing that engagement with the intervention is critical in realizing potential positive outcomes. The findings suggest that access and usage barriers should be considered when designing interventions and that behavioral nudges may serve to increase engagement.

Introduction

Around 250 million children globally under the age of 5 are at risk of poor developmental outcomes, including social-emotional and cognitive skills foundational to learning and academic success (Lu et al., 2016). This issue disproportionately affects low-and middle-income countries in the Majority Worldfoot_0 , where poverty-related factors create barriers for early childhood development. In South Africa, poverty hinders the quality of parent-child interactions that scaffold development by limiting learning resources in the home (e.g., lack of reading material).

Roughly 68% of children in South Africa live in poverty (Hall, 2025) and 46% of children under age five are already behind on developmental milestones (e.g., social-emotional learning [SEL], language, cognitive, and early literacy and numeracy skills; Tredoux et al., 2024).

Positive home learning environments and activities such as shared book reading promote early childhood development, particularly for children in higher-risk low-resource contexts.

However, implementing positive parenting practices can be challenging for parents precisely from such contexts. Educational technologies (EdTech) have been promoted as a useful tool to support parents with reading resources and activities that advance child development. Indeed, research on the positive use of EdTech such as digital books for young children in diverse contexts has begun to accumulate (see Kucirkova, 2018, for an overview). However, this evidence base remains limited and rigorously designed impact evaluations of EdTech (i.e., randomized control trials; RCTs) are scant (Silverman et al., 2025). Recent work has called for the need to evaluate EdTech intervention studies on multiple indicators of quality, including their methodological quality, generalizability, and transparency (Kucirkova et al., 2023). Where evidence does exist, it is often limited to high-income countries in the Minority World instead of low-resource contexts with a disproportionate burden of low child development outcomes.

Beyond these challenges, when positive impacts of EdTech have been demonstrated in context, user engagement remains an issue. For example, user retention rates are only about 2% after one month (Curry, 2026), highlighting the need to develop and test strategies that keep parents engaged with tools that have demonstrated positive impact. This study provides an evaluation of a shared book reading and parenting EdTech App (BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM , henceforth abbreviated to BS-VT), and digital engagement strategies for caregivers and their children in South Africa, focusing on impacts on parenting practices and early childhood development.

Parenting and Early Childhood Development

Parenting practices that provide consistent stimulation within a supportive home environment play a central role in shaping children's cognitive, behavioral, and language development (Chang et al., 2009; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [NASEM], 2016). Practices such as shared reading, responsive communication, and developmentally appropriate scaffolding are especially influential because they provide learning opportunities and promote high-quality parent-child interactions. Through experience, observation, feedback, and formal or informal information sources, parents form a system of knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy that shapes their parenting behavior and children's outcomes (Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018; NASEM, 2016). Parents' knowledge of child development, including age-appropriate expectations, strategies, and understanding of child social-emotional and cognitive needs, shapes how these practices are enacted and determines the quality of the home learning environment (NASEM, 2016; September et al., 2016).

Parental knowledge alone does not ensure effective practice, positive beliefs about parenting and parental self-efficacy (PSE) can increase the likelihood that those practices are translated into consistent, evidence-based parenting (NASEM, 2016). PSE stems from accurate developmental knowledge, successful parenting experiences, and beliefs about the value of early investment, which strengthen confidence and persistence in effective parenting practices (Benedetto & Ingrassia, 2018; September et al., 2016).

Parenting practices are highly influenced by socioeconomic status (SES). Low-SES families with limited resources engage in positive parent-child interactions (e.g., activities that promote development) less frequently (Lurie et al., 2021). Lower-SES caregivers also tend to have less knowledge about developmental milestones and how parenting practices positively influence development (Bornstein et al., 2010) and thus, are less likely to believe that early childhood investments influence development (List et al., 2021). EdTech interventions have the potential to address these disparities by providing low-cost, scalable, and accessible guidance that increases caregivers' knowledge, confidence, and opportunities to engage in developmentally supportive interactions with their children, particularly among families with limited access to traditional parenting resources.

EdTech for Parenting and Child Development

Parenting

EdTech interventions can improve parent-child interactions, literacy engagement, parenting knowledge, and PSE, although effects across studies are mixed and not consistently sustained over time (Jäggi et al., 2025; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Lin-Lewry et al., 2024). EdTech interventions related to observable parenting behaviors have been associated with greater caregiver involvement in shared reading and other literacy activities, stronger parent-child interactions, and more frequent use of developmentally supportive parenting practices, such as praise, responsive caregiving, and joint media engagement (Korin, 2021; Jäggi et al., 2025; Richert et al., 2025). For example, Jäggi et al. (2025) reviewed 13 digital parenting interventions and found generally positive effects on literacy engagement and parent-child communication.

However, because the review included mixed study designs, the findings do not consistently support causal conclusions.

Evidence for improvements in PSE is less consistent. In a meta-analysis of seven RCTs involving 1,342 new parents, which evaluated programs delivered through websites and mobile apps focusing on child development, and transition to parenthood, Lin-Lewry et al. (2024) found that EdTech interventions produced significant short-term improvements in PSE, perceived social support, and depressive symptoms. Thus, EdTech interventions may strengthen PSE by giving caregivers opportunities to learn, practice skills, and receive social support (Lin-Lewry et al., 2024). However, effect sizes varied across programs, and some trials found limited or no benefits, particularity for shorter interventions. Overall, factors such as program duration, delivery modality, and the level of user engagement appear to shape both the size and sustainability of parenting outcomes.

Child Development and Learning

Specific types of EdTech can also support children's SEL, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills. For example, children can learn new vocabulary from developmentally appropriate digital media; e-books with interactive features reinforce rather than distract from the story (Richert et al., 2025). Shared parent-child reading of digital books has also been linked to improvements in language and reading (Bus et al., 2025). Some apps also show promise for supporting social-emotional development (Hikmah et al., 2024); EdTech-based interventions have improved attention, impulse control, and adaptability among preschool-aged children (Yao & Abdullah, 2026). In an RCT involving 74 preschoolers, Naumann et al. (2023) found that a six-week digital intervention program improved emotional regulation and reduced behavioral problems compared with a control condition. Hikmah et al. (2024) similarly found greater gains in SEL in children using interactive media than in children using traditional storybooks. More broadly, apps and games built around prosocial content may strengthen empathy, cooperation, conflict resolution, and other social skills while reducing problematic behaviors (Richert et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Hikmah et al., 2024).

Although developmentally-appropriate, research-informed EdTech has demonstrated meaningful benefits for children's learning and development, most commercially available digital products have little evidence of educational effectiveness (Korin, 2021; Richert et al., 2025). For example, an evaluation of the 124 most-downloaded educational apps found that most provided repetitive, distracting, and pedagogically weak experiences with limited learning value (Mayer et al., 2023). Similarly, only one-quarter of the 100 most popular EdTech products used in U.S. schools had empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness (LearnPlatform, n.d.). Impact depends heavily on the quality of the technology, the evidence informing its design, the context in which it is used, caregiver involvement, and sustained user engagement (Richert et al., 2025).

EdTech Engagement

A persistent challenge for EdTech parenting interventions is maintaining caregiver engagement over time. Engagement with EdTech is typically highest immediately following enrollment and declines once its novelty has worn off, limiting opportunities for interventions to influence parenting behaviors and child development (Tsay et al., 2020). Many EdTech interventions incorporate behavioral science-based messaging strategies, or behavioral nudges, to encourage continued use. These strategies are designed to reduce cognitive barriers (e.g., information overload, weariness), increase motivation, and prompt users to engage with the intervention, thereby increasing the likelihood that the intervention will achieve its intended effects (Balaskas et al., 2025). Nudges can be delivered through multiple channels (e.g., push notifications, text messages, emails) and may include simple reminders, or motivational or goal-setting prompts (Duckworth et al., 2025; Mayer et al., 2023; Kalil et al., 2023).

Evidence suggests that the effectiveness of behavioral nudges depends on their content rather than simply their frequency. Messages that target users' motivations or encourage goal setting have been shown to increase engagement more effectively than generic reminder nudges in some studies (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023). Conversely, some studies find that reminders alone can effectively increase engagement (Hansen & Andersen, 2025; York et al., 2019). However, greater engagement does not necessarily translate into impact. For example, although goal-setting nudges increased app use, they did not improve children's literacy outcomes, possibly because caregivers engaged with the app to satisfy the prompts rather than to meaningfully participate in reading activities-a phenomenon described as the "nag factor" (Kalil et al., 2023). Behavioral nudges can be an important strategy for improving engagement, but their effectiveness depends on both the design of the messages and whether they promote meaningful participation rather than simply increasing app use. To date, limited empirical work has compared different behavioral nudging strategies on parents' engagement with EdTech, and in turn, impacts on parenting practices and child outcomes.

Current Study

The current study is a mixed-methods evaluation of BookSmart with built-in parenting tips (Vroom Tips TM ) and its impact on caregivers' self-efficacy, caregiving beliefs and practices, and early childhood outcomes (including SEL and problem behaviors, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills) in South Africa (Worldreader, n.d.; Vroom, n.d.).

The BookSmart application, developed by Worldreader, is a digital reading platform designed as a literacy-focused intervention that provides children-particularly those in low-resource settings-with access to reading materials. BookSmart aims to achieve four primary goals: (1) to foster caregiver-child engagement in home reading, (2) to strengthen caregivers' self-efficacy in shared reading, (3) to promote children's early literacy development by emphasizing the pivotal role of caregivers in shaping early literacy experiences, and (4) to provide children with access to literary resources. BookSmart also serves as a digital platform that includes access to Vroom's science-based parenting content (Vroom Tips TM ). This enhanced version of the BookSmart platform embeds Vroom's practical "Brain Building" prompts within the reading experience. Prompts were brief, play-based, and evidence-informed activities designed to help caregivers promote learning and development during everyday shared moments.

For example, "Snack Sorters" prompts children to group snacks together, encouraging them to learn shapes and colours (see Methods for more details). Activities of this type support observational skills, language development, and interactive engagement. The integration aims to simultaneously promote shared reading, strengthen caregiver-child relationships, and support early brain and literacy development.

Evidence from a previous evaluation in Kenya demonstrated that engagement with BookSmart effectively increased the frequency of parent-child reading interactions in the home.

Over 22 weeks, the frequency of reading with their child significantly increased and children's emergent literacy and vocabulary skills significantly improved (Kucirkova et al., 2025). Total time spent reading was positively associated with improvements in children's pre-literacy skills.

Significant gains were also observed in children's social-emotional outcomes (Kucirkova et al., 2025). However, maintaining caregiver engagement within the app remained a key challenge: caregiver-engagement with the app significantly decreased after 3 weeks of use, which could have diminished potential positive impacts (Kucirkova et al., 2025).

This study extends prior work by testing specific behavioral nudging strategies to increase caregiver engagement: reminder and goal-setting nudges. Two studies were conducted: a 4-arm RCT to evaluate the impact of BS-VT with different behavioral nudging strategies, and a qualitative study to explore caregivers' experiences and challenges with the app.

Study 1: Impact Evaluation of BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM with Behavioral Nudging

Participants were randomized into four groups: BS-VT with goal-setting nudges, BS-VT with reminder nudges, BS-VT (no behavioral nudges), and a wait-listed control group. We asked the following research questions: (1) Does BS-VT impact caregivers' self-efficacy, and caregiving beliefs and practices, and children's early childhood development (SEL and problem behaviors, cognitive, language, and early literacy and numeracy skills)?

(2) Do caregivers' use and engagement with BS-VT impact caregivers' self-efficacy, and caregiving beliefs and practices and impact children's early development?

(3) Do different behavioral nudging strategies (reminder nudges versus goal-setting nudges) impact caregivers' use and engagement with BS-VT?

Based on BookSmart's previous evaluation in Kenya, we predicted that caregiver's beliefs will positively shift following the use of BS-VT (Kucirkova et al., 2025). Children's developmental scores and caregiver self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices were predicted to improve following increased use and engagement with BS-VT. Additionally, we predicted that use and engagement with BS-VT will improve with the addition of behavioral nudges. Based on our theory of change (Figure 1), behavioral nudges would boost app usage, increasing positive caregiving processes, thereby impacting child developmental outcomes. Study 2: Caregiver Experiences Using BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM Interviews with 20 caregivers further explored the role of BS-VT in households and caregivers' experiences with the app. We asked: (1) in the context of everyday family life, how do caregivers describe their experience with the usability of BS-VT, (2) what challenges do caregivers face incorporating BS-VT into their daily routines, and (3) what suggestions do caregivers have for improving BS-VT use in real-life family settings?

This study aimed to address important gaps in the EdTech literature by providing a rigorous mixed-methods evaluation of an evidence-informed digital book reading and parenting intervention. By combining experimental estimates of impact with qualitative insights into caregiver experiences, we examined whether BS-VT improves caregiver and child outcomes and how engagement influences its effectiveness. In doing so, we contribute to the limited evidence base on EdTech in low-resource settings, informing the design and implementation of scalable digital interventions for young children and their families.

Study 1: Impact Evaluation of BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM with Behavioral Nudging

Methods

Participants

Caregivers who had at least one child between 3-5 years old residing in South Africa were recruited into the study in January 2026. Prospective participants received a study invitation link randomized to one of four conditions: access to BS-VT and prompted with reminder nudges, access to the BS-VT and prompted with goal-setting nudges, access to the BS-VT app alone, or given no access to the BS-VT app. These groups are henceforth referred to as the treatment groups (Reminder Nudges, Goal-Setting Nudges, BookSmart Alone, respectively), and the control group. 812 participants enrolled in the study and completed a baseline survey, see Figure 2. Attrition led to a final sample size of 519 participants (M age = 4.33 years, SD age = 0.80, range = 2.97-6.00) who completed both baseline and endline surveys, see Figure 2. Attrition did not differ between groups (F(3, 808) = 1.23, p = .299). Note that higher SES predicted endline survey completion (β = 0.61, SE = 0.14, t = 4.35, p < .001). Caregivers were recruited through MoyaApp, a free-to-download super app in South Africa that houses BS-VT as a mini app, enabling data-free access for families and addressing access in underserved communities for whom data costs are a significant barrier. See Supplementary Methods for details about MoyaApp and recruitment process. A power analysis (β = 0.9) determined that a sample of 634 participants was necessary to detect a small effect (MDES f = 0.15). The final sample of 519 corresponds to a MDES of 0.166. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework Note. Participants who enrolled in the study (enrolled sample), completed both baseline and endline measures (final sample), accessed BS-VT, and engaged with BS-VT. Despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention (n = 30 engaged with BookSmart content).

Inclusion & Exclusion Criteria

Families were excluded from the study if they did not have a child between ages 3 to 5.

Caregivers that had never used MoyaApp or had not been active on the platform in the last 30 days were also excluded. Families were also ineligible if they had previously used BS-VT in the last 6 months. Finally, caregivers must have responded to the MoyaApp survey indicating interest in participating in the study to be included. Children with developmental disabilities, including autism spectrum disorder, down syndrome, fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, fragile X syndrome, cerebral palsy, and ADHD, were included in the study.

Procedure

All measures were administered through a REDCap survey (Harris et al., 2009; 2019).

Data were collected at baseline (January-March 2026) and endline (May-June 2026). After completing the baseline survey, participants in the BS-VT treatment conditions were prompted to create a user profile and begin using the app. The control group received a prompt to create a user profile and use the BS-VT app after endline data was collected. After the intervention period, all participants who completed the baseline survey were sent a link to the endline survey through MoyaApp messaging. Participants who completed both surveys were compensated with vouchers worth 90-100 2 South African rand that could be used to purchase products and services offered through MoyaApp (e.g., airtime, entertainment, bus tickets, etc.).

Intervention

Caregivers used the BS-VT EdTech app (see Figure 2) for ~12 weeks between January and June 2026 (due to the rolling enrollment period [January 22-March 17], caregivers received between 11 and 22 weeks of the intervention [M = 15.64, SD = 2.34], depending on when they joined the study and initialized their BS-VT profile). Participants in the control group had their access to the app blocked for the intervention duration. Additionally, caregivers were unable to access the BookSmart app for 2 weeks in March 2026.

Behavioral nudges.

Participants in in the goal-setting and reminder nudges groups received 3-4 behavioral nudges per week that varied by style: basic text messages, messages containing Vroom Tip TM modeling videos (e.g., characters from the Kooky Kitty Worldreader Original book series, Mommy Kitty and Kooky Kitty, completing a Vroom Tip TM together), and messages containing animations of characters from the Kooky Kitty Worldreader Original book series (Figure 3). In a typical week, participants received one basic text message, one modeling video, and two animation messages. Behavioral nudges were sent on Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday (day of each message style varied week to week). Note, neither the goal-setting nor reminder nudges groups received video messages for a few weeks in April 2026 due to a technical error.

2 Participants were typically compensated 90 rand. In the remaining week of endline data collection, participants who had not yet completed their endline survey were sent a reminder message to finish the survey with a bonus 10 rand offer. This was done to incentivize survey completion.

48 different Reminder Nudges (e.g., "Kooky has some ideas on the Booksmart app for making cleaning up fun today!"), and 48 different Goal-Setting Nudges (e.g., "Let's play! When will you try a brainy playtime tip from BookSmart this weekend? Maybe while getting dressed or cleaning up?") were generated that were inspired by previous studies (e.g., Duckworth et al., 2025; Mayer et al. 2023; Kalil et al., 2023) and content of the modeling videos, animations, in-app Vroom Tips TM , and BookSmart reading material. After an initial list of messages was created, Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft, 2025) was used to help brainstorm additional message content and ensure the language conformed to a 5th grade reading level. Messages were reviewed and revised by a leading expert in behavioral science-based messaging interventions, and edited for style by the MoyaApp Communications team to ensure cultural relevance. Note. BookSmart app and characters from the Worldreader Original series. (A)

The BookSmart contains reading resources and family activities on its home page. (B) Vroom Tips TM are separated into categories (e.g., snacktime, playtime), and include a "Tip of the Day" that describes an activity designed to promote childhood development, along with an explanation of the skills their child may learn. (C) Still images of the modeling videos in the study, consisting of characters from the Kooky Kitty Worldreader Original series completing a Vroom Tip TM.

Measures

Demographic Information (Baseline Only)

We collected general information, including caregiver and child age, caregiver's gender, race/ethnic heritage, where they live, languages they speak, and caregiver relation to child (e.g., biological mother, father, etc.). Due to experimental error, we did not collect data on child gender. We collected information about the child's development (e.g., caregiver concern about hearing, sight, and speech) and whether the child has been diagnosed with a developmental disorder. The survey also collected SES information, including caregivers' education level, household monthly income, and a household inventory (e.g., washing machine, TV set, computer). The Macarthur Scale of Subjective Social Status was also used to assess perceived SES compared to others in South Africa, and their community (Adler et al., 2000).

Caregiver Measures

The Self-Efficacy for Parenting Tasks Index (SEPTI; Davison et al., 2024) assessed caregiver self-efficacy in language-and reading-related activities, caregiver history of language and reading difficulties, shared caregiver-child reading time, learning techniques used in the home, and household access to children's books. Responses were scored on a 6-point scale from "strongly disagree," to "strongly agree". Higher scores indicated greater perceived caregiving competence. Caregiver history of language and reading difficulties were assessed at baseline; all other areas were assessed at both time points. (Attanasio et al., 2019), assessed caregivers' perceived importance of caregiver-child interactions for children's educational attainment. Caregivers completed hypothetical scenarios estimating the percentage of children who would achieve a specified level of education under interactive versus non-interactive caregiving conditions.

Subjective caregiver beliefs

Higher scores indicate stronger beliefs that caregiver engagement influences child outcomes.

UNICEF's Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS): Base Questionnaire for Children

Under 5 assessed caregiving practices, including cognitive stimulation and caregiver engagement in the home. Caregivers were asked six questions about whether or not they or any other adult engaged in various activities (e.g., reading) with the child over the previous 3 days. Responses were scored as either 2 for yes or 1 for no, and then summed.

The Brigance Parent-Child Interactions Scale (BPCIS; Glascoe & Brigance, 2002)

assessed caregiver-child interactions and classified households as resilient, at risk, or neutral.

Caregivers rated interaction scenarios (e.g., I help my child learn by talking and showing him or her new things) using frequency response scales (e.g., "not very often," "sometimes," "often,"; "not very true," "not very true," "sometimes true," "mostly true.").

Child Measures

The Parents' Evaluation of Developmental Status: Developmental Milestones (PEDS:DM) assessed children's social-emotional, expressive and receptive language, and early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills. For social-emotional and language skills, all tasks were administered and scored according to the PEDS:DM protocols, yielding separate scores for social-emotional skills, expressive language, and receptive language. For academic skills, question 1 ("If you showed your child a penny and asked, 'What's this?', would he or she say penny or cent?") was omitted due to relevance concerns, as such, all children began with item 2.

The Ages and Stages Questionnaire, Third Edition (ASQ-3) assessed children's personal

social, problem solving (cognitive), and communication skills. Caregivers were presented with scenarios of things their child may be able to do, or were prompted to ask their child a question and see how they responded. Caregivers indicated whether their child could do each scenario with "yes" (10 points), "no" (0 points), or "sometimes" (5 points). Points were summed for a final score in each domain, with higher scores indicating stronger skills. Domain scores were then standardized according to the child's age group so scores could be compared across ages.

The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) assessed children's social-emotional well-being and difficulties using age-appropriate caregiver-report items. Caregivers rated each item as "not true," "somewhat true," or "certainly true." Items were scored on a three-point scale, with positively worded items reverse-scored where required. Scores were calculated for emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behavior.

Internalizing difficulties were calculated as sum of emotional and peer-problem scores, and externalizing difficulties as sum of conduct and hyperactivity scores. Higher prosocial scores indicated prosocial behavior; higher scores on all other domains indicated greater difficulties. Supplementary Materials provide further details on caregiver and child measures.

BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM Usage and Engagement

BS-VT usage metrics were tracked for each participant during the intervention period: (1) the number of times the app was used, (2) the total time (seconds) spent in the app, the number of completed (3) books and (4) Vroom Tips TM . See Supplementary Materials for details.

Data Analysis

We first tested baseline equivalence of the four treatment groups using an analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each child and caregiver outcome and SES (see Tables S3-S7). We also conducted Pearson's correlations of caregiver-and child-level outcomes and BS-VT engagement.

To address our first research question (intent-to-treat; ITT), we used multiple regression models with planned contrasts to examine whether treatment group predicted endline caregiver-and child-level outcomes, with baseline score, child age, and SES included as covariates. Condition contrast vector was specified to contrast (1) no treatment (control group) versus treatment groups, (2) no behavioral nudges (BookSmart Alone group) versus behavioral nudges (Reminder and Goal-Setting Nudges groups), and (3) Reminder Nudges versus Goal-Setting Nudges.

To address our second research question (treatment-on-the-treated; ToT), we used multiple regression models to examine whether engagement with BS-VT (i.e., completing books or Vroom Tips TM ) predicted endline caregiver-and child-level outcomes, with baseline score, child age, and SES included as covariates. Separate models were conducted using a binomial variable indicating whether the caregiver had any or no engagement, number of completed books, and number of completed Vroom Tips TM.

To address our third research question, we examined whether behavioral nudges (i.e., Goal-Setting Nudges, Reminder Nudges, no nudges) predicted engagement. Separate models were conducted using a binomial variable indicating whether the caregiver had any or no engagement, number of completed books, and number of completed Vroom Tips TM as outcomes.

Where applicable, zero-inflated Poisson regression models were used to account for the high proportion of zero scores (n BookZeros = 267 [71%], n VroomTipsZeros = 309 [83%]).

All analyses were conducted using R (v4.5.1; R Core Team, 2025). Caregiver outcomes were self-efficacy, beliefs about caregiver-child interactions, and caregiving practices. Child outcomes were SEL and problem behaviors, cognition, language, and early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills. Supplementary Materials provide additional details on constructs.

Separate models testing interactions between treatment group (question 1), or engagement (question 2) and age, SES, and baseline score, respectively, were conducted to examine treatment variation and are reported in Supplementary Materials. To account for multiple comparisons, q values were generated within prespecified families of related hypotheses grouped by research question using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction (Benjamin & Hochberg, 1995); see Supplementary Materials for details.

Results

Detailed descriptive statistics are reported in Tables S3-S17. 19 caregivers reported that their child had been diagnosed with at least one disability or disorder, see Table S18 for S19. Figure 4 reports the correlations between caregiver-and child-level outcomes and engagement with BS-VT. Note. Correlations exclude participants from the control group. Correlations between (A) baseline and (B) endline caregiver-level and child-level measures with engagement data.

Insignificant values (p > .05) are blank. Correlations between supplementary measures are reported in Supplementary Materials (Figure S1).

RQ 1: Impact of BookSmart & Vroom Tips TM on Caregiving and Child Development

Caregiver Outcomes

Caregivers in treatment groups reported marginally higher self-efficacy than the control group, however, this finding was no longer marginal after correcting for multiple comparisons (Table 1, Panel A). No other significant main effects of treatment status on caregivers were found. A significant interaction between baseline caregiver beliefs and treatment status (β(SE) = -0.06(0.03), p = .011; q = .042; Table S21) revealed that treatment vs. control marginally decreased beliefs for caregivers with higher baseline beliefs (+1SD below mean beliefs: β(SE) = -24.79(11.86), p = .075). Secondary analyses compared differences across treatment groups for individual variables. Families in the treatment conditions versus control group had significantly higher shared caregiver-child reading time (β(SE) = 0.03(0.01), p = .020; q = .098; Table S29), however, this finding became marginal after correcting for multiple comparisons.

Child Outcomes

No significant main effects of treatment status on child outcomes were found. Interaction effects (see Table S23, S26, and S27) showed that treatment, receiving nudges, and nudge type (goal-setting versus reminder) increased child outcomes for younger children, children from low-SES families, and children with lower baseline scores.

Socioemotional skills.

A marginally significant interaction between baseline SEL score and treatment status (β(SE) = 0.15(0.07), p = .025; q = 0.82; Table S23), revealed that goal-setting versus reminder nudges marginally increased SEL for children with lower baseline SEL scores (-1SD below mean SEL score: β(SE) = -0.27(0.13), p = .084).

Cognitive skills.

Interactions (Table S26) between treatment status and age (β(SE) = -0.01(0.00), p = .011; q = .042), SES (β(SE) = -0.12(0.05), p = .027; q = .088), and baseline cognitive skills (β(SE) = 0.15(0.07), p = .032; q = .100) revealed increased cognitive skills for treatment versus control groups in younger children (-1SD below mean age: β(SE) = 0.94(0.40), p = .040), nudges vs. no nudges in children from low SES families (-1SD below mean SES: β(SE) = 0.62(0.30), p = .085), and for goal-setting vs. reminder nudges in children with low baseline cognitive skills (-1SD below mean cognitive skills: β(SE) = 0.41(018), p = .054).

Language skills. Interactions (Table S27) between baseline language score and nudges (Nudges vs. No Nudges: β(SE) = -0.08(0.03), p = .024; q = 0.79; Reminder vs. Goal-Setting: β(SE) = 15(0.06), p = .010; q = 0.40), revealed that nudges increased language skills in children with low baseline language skills (-1SD below mean language skill; Nudges vs. No Nudges: β(SE) = 0.46(0.21), p = .056; Goal-Setting vs. Reminder: β(SE) = 0.24(0.12), p = .111foot_2 ).

RQ 2: BookSmart & Vroom Tips TM Engagement and Caregiving and Child Development

Caregiver Outcomes

Completing a higher number of Vroom Tips TM was significantly associated with lower caregiver self-efficacy (Table 2, Panel C). Interactions between baseline caregiver scores and number of Vroom Tips completed (self-efficacy: β(SE) = -0.02(0.01), p = .006; q = .030; interaction beliefs: β(SE) = -0.02(0.01), p = .020; q = .084; Table S41 and S42) revealed that a higher number of completed Vroom Tips was associated with significantly lower caregiver self-efficacy and caregiver interaction beliefs for caregivers who reported high self-efficacy and beliefs, respectively, at baseline (+1SD above mean baseline self efficacy: β(SE) = -0.17(0.03), p < .001; +1SD above mean baseline beliefs: β(SE) = -1.14(0.38), p = .003). Secondary analyses showed that BS-VT engagement and number of Vroom Tips completed predicted increased cognitive stimulation and caregiver engagement in the home (Table S52).

Child Outcomes

Families who completed more books reported significantly higher language skills (Table 4, Panel B) and participants who engaged with BS-VT reported significantly higher child academic skills, however, this finding became marginal after correcting for multiple comparisons (Table 4, Panel A). Secondary analyses also found that the number of books completed significantly predicted increased child expressive language skills (Table S58).

Research Question 3 -Impact of Engagement Strategies (Reminder Nudges Versus

Goal-Setting Nudges) on Caregivers' BookSmart and Vroom Tips TM Use and Engagement

Caregivers in the Goal-Setting Nudges group were more likely to have engaged with BS-VT compared to participants in the Reminder Nudges group, however, this finding was no longer significant after correcting for multiple comparisons (Table 5, Panel A). Caregivers who received behavioral nudges completed marginally more books and significantly more Vroom Tips TM than caregivers who received no behavioral nudge (Table 5, Panel B). Caregivers in the Goal-Setting Nudges group completed significantly more Vroom Tips TM than caregivers in the Reminder Nudges group (Table 5, Panel C).
