Study 2: Qualitative Study

Methods

Participants

We recruited 20 caregivers through MoyaApp, as in study 1, and followed the same inclusion and exclusion criteria with the following addition: families were excluded from the study if the caregiver was not female and between the ages 18 to 45. A sample of 20 was selected with the intention of the study being exploratory. Most in-depth interview studies achieve saturation with samples of 9-17 (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022), suggesting that our sample size should have provided sufficient results. 7 participants were caregivers of 3 year olds, 5 were caregivers of 4 year olds, and 8 were caregivers of 5 year olds.

Measures

Interview Questions

The baseline interviews established what caregivers were already doing in their daily lives to help their child learn, and how capable they felt doing so. In other words, the baseline interviews surfaced caregivers' starting point: their habits, mindsets, and gaps before exposure to BS-VT. We asked caregivers about their daily interactions and shared reading routines and whether/how they integrated digital tools into these routines. We also asked caregivers about their feelings of confidence and/or support needs for helping their child learn new things, and their beliefs about the importance of these everyday interactions for helping their child learn.

The endline interviews were both evaluative (did BS-VT add value?) and generative (what lessons and incentive structures can inform future iterations?). We asked caregivers how they and their child used and felt about BS-VT, and the extent to which the tools fit into their daily routine. We also asked the caregivers about their feelings towards the nudges, to understand whether the messages helped promote app usage. Finally, we asked caregivers about their feelings of confidence and/or support needs for helping their child learn new things, their beliefs about the importance of these everyday interactions for helping their child learn, and how using BS-VT impacted their feelings of confidence, needs, and beliefs. See Supplementary Materials for the complete baseline and endline interview questions.

BookSmart Engagement

BS-VT usage metrics were tracked for each participant, including the number of times the app was used, the total time (seconds) spent in the app, the number of books completed, and the number of Vroom Tips TM completed.

Procedures

Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025. Afterwards, they were prompted to use BS-VT for an intervention period of 3 weeks.

Data Analysis

The interviews were coded by four members of the research team using Dedoose software (Dedoose Version 10.0.59, 2025) and following a combination deductive-inductive thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The interview questions were based on the mechanisms by which EdTech and caregiving practices relate to child learning and development outcomes, as illuminated by existing academic literature (e.g., self-efficacy, beliefs, knowledge, shared reading, caregiving practices, app engagement, accessibility). An initial set of a priori codes was generated based on the content of the interviews and the aforementioned mechanisms of interest. The a priori codes were grouped according to a priori themes developed based on our research questions. See Supplementary Materials for details.

Results

Usage and Engagement

Usage varied widely. App usage declined slightly over the course of the intervention period, however, the average number of books completed increased. Some participants used the app very little, while others spent significant amounts of time in the app and completed several books and Vroom Tips TM . Importantly, Vroom Tips TM usage was quite low overall. The vast majority of participants did not open or complete any Vroom Tips TM . Table S62 provides

Semi-Structured Interviews

Baseline Findings

Motivation is Academic ('School Readiness'). The interviews suggested that caregivers were highly motivated to read with their child. Caregivers saw a direct link between reading and speech and vocabulary skill development, and their motivation was driven by a desire for children to master the English language and succeed in Grade R (i.e., compulsory year of education prior to Grade 1). Participant Q040 reflected, "My five-year-old didn't speak or utter many words… So I started reading. Then yes, his tongue became easier to say [words]." Overall, it seemed that caregivers viewed shared reading as more of an educational duty instead of a recreational or bonding activity.

The Confidence-Support Paradox. The interviews illuminated an interesting contradiction related to caregiver confidence and self-efficacy. Caregivers felt confident in their ability to support their child's learning and development. However, they explicitly requested support in the form of guidance or reminders. Participant Q049 said, "Yes, I do feel confident… [my child] react[s] when I'm playing with them, when I'm teaching them", but also explained that being too busy limits their everyday interactions with their child, and expressed a desire for resources on how to better support their child's learning. In other words, their confidence was high, but they also needed support. These findings suggest that although caregivers feel capable of supporting their child's learning, the logistics of everyday life overwhelm their capabilities.

The Resource Gap and 'Latent Demand'. Not only did they feel overwhelmed, but caregivers also noted significant gaps in physical reading and learning resources. Most of the caregivers reported that their households owned fewer than three children's books; they often relied on books and materials sent home from school. They also mentioned the cost of books and fatigue from working late shifts as barriers to shared reading. Caregivers expressed that they wanted to read more frequently, even daily, if it were not for these barriers. Participant Q034 told us, "If I had more books and more time, I would read every day. But right now, we just have the school books." These barriers may have contributed to caregivers' perception of shared reading being purely a means to a developmental end; they did not have the time, energy, or resources for shared reading to be a fun, recreational activity.

Digital Hesitancy and the Data Barrier.

Moreover, although smartphones were ubiquitous among the caregivers we interviewed, they were not viewed as reading and learning resources. Prior to the BS-VT intervention, caregivers and their children primarily used devices for passive entertainment, such as watching cartoons on YouTube. Due to the high cost of cellular data in South Africa, caregivers expressed hesitance about depleting their airtime by clicking unknown links or exploring new educational apps. Data cost is therefore a major barrier for caregivers who might otherwise seek out digital resources to supplement the few physical books and learning resources they have in their home. Thus, the data-free nature of the MoyaApp environment is a crucial prerequisite for engagement with apps like BookSmart, making them accessible regardless of cost barriers.

Learning Integrated into Daily Routines.

Since households had limited reading and educational materials and toys, caregivers relied heavily on everyday household activities and routines to provide incidental learning opportunities for their child. Caregivers told us they count vegetables while cooking, name colors while doing laundry, and sing songs while completing chores with their child. They also cited unstructured outdoor play as the primary method of promoting their child's physical and social development.

Endline Findings

The 'Digital Unlock': Access Trumps Preference. Although some caregivers reported feeling a sentimental preference for physical books, they were driven to use BookSmart by the convenience it offered. Participant Q078 expressed a preference for physical books, but also showed appreciation for BookSmart by saying, "they have a lot of books… there's a variety of choice… [and] we don't have access to a library". With BookSmart, caregivers were able to "carry a library" in their pocket, allowing them to read with their child during idle moments when they previously would not have. The participants also appreciated the sheer volume of diverse children's stories available, feeling that BookSmart addressed the reading resource scarcity they felt prior to the intervention period. The intervention seemed to shift caregivers' perceptions of the smartphone as a passive entertainment device to an educational tool.

Hybrid Habits and Physical Interaction.

Caregivers relayed that the app did not replace physical interactions and books. Some caregivers mentioned that their children wanted to turn pages or touch the phone while reading, or take the phone outside like they would with physical books; things they are unable to do with their caregivers' smartphone. A few caregivers also discussed the challenge of "shared focus" on a small screen, with notifications and incoming calls sometimes disrupting the reading flow. It seems that BookSmart did not replace physical books, but it did supplement the reading resources they were lacking and provided benefits that physical books could not, like the ability to read anywhere and anytime.

Validation of Behavioral Nudges.

Overall, caregivers appreciated the reminders to use BS-VT. They saw the reminders as helpful prompts that supported their ability to create a habit out of using BS-VT with their child. However, a minority of participants did not see the messages, which may have limited their app usage. As participant Q054 explained, "I didn't see the messages… if I had the reminder, I would have remembered to read more." This may have been due to individual user's MoyaApp notification settings.

The Language Barrier and the 'Translation Burden'. Despite the overall positive experience that caregivers had with BookSmart, a major friction point was the dominance of English reading content. South Africa is a multilingual country, and many children are native speakers of a non-English language (e.g., isiZulu, isiXhosa, Venda, etc.) which may be the primary language spoken in the home. Caregivers reported reading the English text silently and then narrating the story in their home language to help their child understand. Participant Q040 explained, "I read in English and translate into [home language]... it helps them understand, but having books in our language would be better." Caregivers expressed the desire for their children to learn English, the lack of stories in home languages forced caregivers to act as real-time translators, requiring a high cognitive load while reading with their child. There is a clear, unmet demand for content in home languages to make the reading experience more culturally resonant.

Discussion

We examined how caregivers in South Africa engaged with a digital reading and parenting platform, BookSmart with embedded parenting tips-Vroom Tips™ (BS-VT), as a resource for supporting young children's learning through shared book reading and everyday caregiver-child interactions. Across two mixed-methods studies, we focused on how this EdTech parenting intervention impacted caregiver self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and children's early developmental outcomes, as well as factors that supported or constrained engagement.

EdTech parenting interventions are often proposed as a scalable means of expanding developmental opportunities for children in low-resource contexts. Our findings suggest that this promise depends on an important distinction between access to developmental resources and engagement in developmentally-supportive experiences. Providing caregivers with access to BS-VT produced limited impacts on caregiver and child outcomes, however, nudging caregivers to engage with BS-VT produced positive child outcomes, including stronger academic (early literacy and numeracy), cognitive, and language skills, specifically for more vulnerable children (i.e., children from lower-SES families and children with lower baseline skills)-albeit these effects were mostly marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and did not meet our threshold for statistical significance (q < .05). Viewed alongside caregivers' accounts of the practical and contextual barriers that shaped BS-VT engagement, these findings suggest that the potential of EdTech parenting interventions to influence child development depends on whether families can integrate parenting content into sustained, meaningful caregiver-child interactions. This distinction is particularly relevant in contexts where socioeconomic disadvantage can constrain developmental opportunities and families face greater barriers to consistently enacting developmentally-supportive practices.

Engagement with Digital Parenting Interventions can Support Children's Development

Simply having access to EdTech resources did not produce positive outcomes in caregiving practices or child outcomes. However, caregiver engagement with BS-VT was marginally linked to higher literacy and numeracy skills, and reading more books significantly predicted higher language skills. These findings add to the growing body of research suggesting that EdTech tools can successfully support early child development (Hikmah et al., 2024; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Richert et al., 2025), but they critically emphasize the need for sustained engagement. A substantial body of research has established that shared reading, responsive communication, and cognitively stimulating activities support children's language, cognitive, and social-emotional development by providing opportunities for learning within everyday caregiver-child interactions (e.g., NASEM, 2016). EdTech parenting interventions may help facilitate these processes by providing caregivers with accessible reading materials, developmentally appropriate activities, and practical guidance for incorporating learning opportunities into daily routines.

Interestingly, while completing parenting tips was positively associated with child outcomes, we found that when caregivers with a higher baseline self-efficacy completed more parenting tips, they were more likely to report lower self-efficacy at endline. Before using BS-VT, interviews with caregivers revealed they felt confident in their caregiving abilities, but desired more support in the form of resources and time. It's possible that after using Vroom Tips TM -which are activities designed to help promote development during brief everyday shared moments-caregivers became exposed to new information about parenting practices, which may have altered caregivers understanding of effective parenting and the standards against which they evaluate their own practice, leading to an adjustment in their self-efficacy. Caregiver-child interactions are shaped by a complex interplay of caregivers' developmental knowledge, self-efficacy, opportunities to engage in supporting parenting practices, and beliefs about the importance of such practices. Parenting interventions often aim to strengthen these constructs simultaneously, however, changes in knowledge and practices may not immediately correspond to improvements in parenting efficacy. This highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of how digital parenting interventions influence the interrelated processes of acquiring developmental knowledge, adopting new parenting practices, and evaluating one's own parenting competence. Future research should examine how these processes unfold over time.

Behavioral Nudges Increased Digital Parenting Tool Engagement and Child Outcomes

A persistent challenge for digital parenting interventions is translating initial access into sustained engagement. Previous research has documented substantial declines in engagement with EdTech interventions over time, potentially limiting their ability to produce sustained changes in parenting practices and child development (Kucirkova et al., 2025). This challenge may be particularly consequential for parenting interventions, where developmental benefits are expected to accumulate through repeated opportunities for responsive interaction and cognitive stimulation rather than isolated exposure to intervention content. Implementing behavioral nudging strategies that can produce sustained engagement into digital parenting tools is therefore key. Engagement with BS-VT overall remained low in this study, with 52% of treated participants having accessed the app and only 39% of those who accessed it read a book or completed a parenting tip. However, caregivers who received nudges completed more parenting tips (q <. 05) and read more books (q < .1) compared to caregivers who were not nudged. This adds to an emerging literature showing that nudge-based parenting interventions can change parental investments and child outcomes, including in the United States (York et al., 2019), Brazil (Bettinger et al., 2022), and Costa Rica (Angrist et al., 2022).

Importantly, the format of the behavioral nudge mattered. Caregivers who received goal-setting nudges completed more parenting tips than caregivers who received reminder nudges, suggesting that goal-setting may be more effective at promoting engagement. This corroborates previous studies (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023). For example, Kalil et al. (2023) found that reminder nudges were associated with a decrease in child skills. Unlike repeated reminders, which may feel intrusive or controlling to busy caregivers, the self-endorsed goals in goal-setting nudges may preserve autonomy by allowing caregivers to choose and initiate their own targets. Consistent with self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000), this autonomy-supportive design may sustain motivation and improve engagement without undermining interaction quality (Kalil et al., 2023; Balaskas et al., 2025). Overall, caregiver interviews indicated that they appreciated the nudges they received, and felt they were useful.

Care was taken to create engaging messages that included animations, parenting modeling videos, and novel content that did not repeat across messages. These strategies may offer a viable solution for promoting engagement with interventions that improve child outcomes.

Importantly, not only did goal-setting nudges increase caregiver engagement, but they made a meaningful impact on children's outcomes. The "fade-in" hypothesis suggests that intervention impacts become detectable only after participants have integrated new practices into their daily routine (Mayer et al., 2023)-our findings suggest goal-setting nudges support this integration and may have been particularly useful for families navigating competing demands associated with socioeconomic disadvantage. Here, we found that children from lower SES households and children with low baseline scores showed positive impacts in social-emotional, cognitive, and language skills when caregivers received behavioral nudges, albeit these effects were largely marginally significant (q < .1). Similarly, a SMS-based parent nudging intervention in Côte d'Ivoire showed no overall impacts on child learning outcomes, yet subgroup analyses revealed that nudges produced larger improvements in learning specifically for children with low baseline learning levels (Wolf & Lichand, 2023).

Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with disparities in access to learning materials and opportunities for cognitively stimulating caregiver-child interactions, contributing to inequalities in early developmental outcomes, even when caregivers recognize the importance of supporting their children's development (Lurie et al., 2021; NASEM, 2016). By providing low-cost access to reading resources and developmentally appropriate parenting activities, EdTech interventions may help address some of the material constraints on the home learning environment, highlighting the potential of digital parenting interventions to reduce inequalities in children's developmental opportunities. However, the same socioeconomic conditions that increase the potential value of EdTech interventions may also constrain families' ability to benefit from them. Access to a platform does not necessarily imply equitable opportunities for meaningful engagement. Differences in device availability and quality, connectivity, digital literacy, language accessibility, and competing household demands may influence whether caregivers can incorporate EdTech resources into everyday routines. Indeed, our finding that SES predicted completion of parenting tips suggests that engagement with EdTech interventions is socio-economically driven. Interviews with caregivers corroborate these challenges: caregivers noted their hesitation around depleting their airtime, highlighting the importance of offering cost-free access, particularly for low-SES families. Language barriers also served as a challenge for caregivers-half reported that they translated stories for their children in real time. BookSmart consists of English-dominant content, while South Africa is highly multilingual with 12 official languages and many additional languages spoken throughout the country. Digital parenting interventions face an important equity challenge: while they may expand opportunities for disadvantaged children, unequal engagement could reproduce or exacerbate existing inequalities.

Implications

A central implication of our findings is that EdTech tools, such as BS-VT, can support parenting and early childhood development (Hikmah et al., 2024; Kucirkova et al., 2025; Naumann et al., 2023; Richert et al., 2025), but engagement with the intervention is critical to realizing positive outcomes. Targeting user engagement is a key determinant of an intervention's effectiveness; even well-designed, evidence-based EdTech applications are unlikely to improve caregiving or child development if users do not engage with them consistently. Behavioral nudges, especially goal-setting prompts, may be particularly helpful for driving engagement (Duckworth et al., 2025; Kalil et al., 2023). Importantly, reducing costs for users to access digital tools can ensure that tools remain equitable and that families can benefit from the learning opportunities they provide, regardless of any socioeconomic barriers.

More broadly, these findings underscore the importance of rigorous, context-sensitive evaluations of digital parenting interventions, particularly in low-resource settings where evidence of effectiveness remains limited. Randomized controlled trials provide an important means of establishing whether EdTech interventions produce measurable improvements in caregiver and child outcomes, while analyses of engagement and qualitative investigations can help identify the processes and contextual conditions that may shape effectiveness.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several important limitations and directions for future research should be considered. Our findings may have been limited by the length of the intervention. The full potential effects of engagement with BS-VT on parenting and child outcomes may require more time to emerge; a longer intervention period may have allowed caregivers more time to integrate BS-VT into their daily routines (Mayer et al., 2023). It's also important to note that several effects did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (q < .05), but were marginally significant (p < .05 and q < .1) and caution should be applied when interpreting these findings. Additionally, engagement data was limited by indicators that captured whether caregivers completed books or parenting tips, but not the quality of engagement. Caregivers may have completed books or parenting tips when children were tired or distracted, with limited conversation or responsive interaction. Engagement may have also been impacted by technical challenges beyond the control of the research team: e.g., some participants in the nudges groups may have not received nudges due their notification settings, potentially limiting their engagement with BS-VT.

Future research should examine how digital parenting interventions become integrated into caregivers' everyday interactions with young children, including how behavioral nudges may shape the frequency and quality of these interactions, and which forms of engagement are most consequential for children's cognitive, language, and social-emotional development. Larger longitudinal studies incorporating multiple measurement points would also help clarify how caregiver and child outcomes evolve as families adopt new parenting practices and identify contextual factors that facilitate or constrain these benefits, particularly in low-resource settings.

Conclusion

These studies (1) evaluated the impact of a digital reading intervention, BookSmart, and its embedded parenting tips, Vroom Tips TM (BS-VT), on caregiver and early childhood outcomes in South Africa and (2) explored the role of behavioral nudging strategies in supporting sustained engagement over time. Our findings show that providing access to EdTech resources alone is insufficient to produce meaningful developmental benefits. Rather, the potential of these interventions depends on caregivers' engagement with developmentally supportive content and opportunities to integrate this content into everyday caregiver-child interactions. Behavioral nudges may help bridge the gap between access and engagement, with our findings suggesting particular potential for supporting children experiencing socioeconomic and developmental disadvantage. By combining experimental estimates of intervention impact with measures of engagement and qualitative accounts of families' experiences, the present study provides insights into both the potential and limitations of digital parenting interventions. Such evaluations are essential for informing the development of interventions that are not only scalable and accessible, but also capable of producing meaningful and equitable developmental benefits.

Supplementary Materials Supplementary Methods

Study 1 -Participant Recruitment MoyaApp is a free-to-download super app in South Africa that features messaging, voice, and video calling capabilities, and houses content, resources, and services (see MoyaApp, n.d.). Importantly, MoyaApp works even when a user has no airtime or data balance, ensuring that access to messaging, resources, and content (including BookSmart) is data free and therefore not cost prohibitive. MoyaApp users can consent to being contacted for research participation during the signup process. An initial screening process was conducted by MoyaApp to identify potential participants who fit the study's eligibility criteria using information provided to MoyaApp as part of the user signup and research contact consent process (i.e., age, caregiver status, BookSmart use, MoyaApp activity). 6000 survey links were generated and randomized to one of four groups: the control group, the BookSmart Alone, the BookSmart and Goal-Setting Messages group, or the BookSmart and Reminder Messages group. 3429 users detected through the initial screening process were sent a survey link through REDCap, a secure, web-based data collection platform (Harris et al., 2009; 2019). Recruitment began January 22, 2026 and was discontinued March 17, 2026 after reaching the target sample size (N = 634). An oversample of 28% (N = 178) was recruited to act as a retention buffer group to account attrition throughout the study; however, attrition was greater than expected due to some technical issues with the app, leading to underpowered analyses.

After opening the baseline survey link, potential participants were required to pass two additional screening checkpoints to ensure we only captured responses from eligible participants. They were first asked to select the age ranges of children they care for. If they indicated they care for a child between 3 to 5 years old, they proceeded to the consent form detailing their participation in the study. In this form, five comprehension questions were administered. If more than two comprehension questions were completed incorrectly, participants were deemed ineligible for the study.

This was done for two primary reasons. First, from an ethical standpoint, it was essential to ensure that all participants were fully informed about the study before providing consent. Incorrect responses indicated that an individual may not have adequately understood the study procedures, risks, or expectations, thereby undermining the validity of their informed consent. Second, adequate reading comprehension was a practical requirement for participation. The study involved caregiver engagement in shared reading activities, a central component of both the intervention and the BookSmart program. Participants who were unable to correctly answer comprehension questions might face challenges in understanding the materials or effectively participating in the reading activities, which could compromise both the fidelity of the intervention and the integrity of the study outcomes.

Those who passed the comprehension questions and consented to the study proceeded to the survey where they were first asked to provide birth dates for their child(ren) between 3 and 5 years old, to confirm that their children are in the target age range. Ineligible participants did not complete the remainder of the survey, which administered all study measures.

Study 1 -Additional Survey Questions

Caregiver education attainment was scored on a scale of 0 to 10, ranging from no schooling to having received a doctorate. Household monthly income was scored on a scale of 0 to 13, ranging from no income to more than R100 000. For each item indicated in the household inventory, one point was assigned for up to 22 points possible. The Macarthur Scale of Subjective Social Status asked caregivers to consider income, education, and employment, then place themself on a ladder depending on where they believed they stood in reference to other people in 1) South Africa, and 2) in their community. The bottom of the ladder (i.e., 1) represented people in the lowest standing, while the top of the ladder (i.e., 10) represented the highest standing (e.g., most money, most education).

The Global Scales for Early Development (GSED) was used to assess generalized development of children up to 36 months of age across diverse cultures and contexts. This assessment was only administered to children aged 3 and older children who scored below age level on the PEDS:DM assessment. We used the short form, caregiver-reported edition of the GSED. Scoring was completed following the instructions provided with the GSED. Note that only 40% of the sample completed the GSED (n = 210) due to the narrower age range and therefore this measure is only reported in the Supplementary Materials.

An additional survey section was administered to the treatment groups at endline to further assess their use of BS-VT. This section asked about: (1) how frequently participants used BookSmart with their child (e.g., every day, once per week, never), (2) how frequently they used Vroom Tips TM (e.g., every day, once per week, never), (3) how frequently they engaged with the in-app suggested activities (i.e., every time, some of the time, or never), and (4) any previous use of BookSmart (i.e., yes or no). This section also asked participants questions about their satisfaction with BS-VT. These questions assessed their (1) overall satisfaction with BS-VT (e.g., somewhat satisfied, accompanied by a written response), (2) reasons as to why they may have not used the app (e.g., not enough time, child does not enjoy it), (3) average comprehension of suggested activities (i.e., always, most of the time, some of the time, or never).

Study 1 -Data Analysis

Tasks

SEPTI: Most area's scores (i.e., caregiver language and reading difficulties, shared caregiver-child reading time, learning techniques used in the home, household access to children's books) were calculated as item means, whereas caregiver self-efficacy was calculated as an item sum.

Subjective Caregiver Beliefs: Three hypothetical scenarios were presented under both conditions (i.e., interactive and non-interactive caregiving). Difference scores between the two conditions were calculated for each scenario and averaged to create a total caregiver involvement belief score. Caregivers had to correctly answer screener questions (i.e., identifying where 25 and 75 were on a slider and which of 25 and 75 were larger) for scores to be included in the relevant analyses.

Constructs

Caregiver outcomes were operationalized as the following constructs: (1) caregiver self-efficacy (SEPTI Caregiver Self-Efficacy), (2) caregiver's beliefs about caregiver-child interactions, and (3) caregiving practices (composite of SEPTI Shared Caregiver-Child Reading Time, SEPTI Learning Techniques Used in the Home, MICS cognitive stimulation and caregiver engagement in the home, and BPCIS household risk, resilience, or neutrality). Child outcomes were operationalized as the following constructs: (1) SEL (composite of PEDS:DM social-emotional skills, SDQ prosocial skills, and ASQ-3 personal social skills measured) and problem behaviors (SDQ internalizing and externalizing difficulties), ( 2) cognition (ASQ-3 child problem solving skills), (3) language (composite of PEDS:DM receptive and expressive language skills, and ASQ-3 communication skills), and (4) early literacy and numeracy (academic) skills (PEDS:DM academic skills). A composite score (composed of the two Macarthur Scale of Subjective Social Status questions, household income, caregiver education, and household amenities) was calculated for household SES to act as a covariate.

Caregiver and child variables that went into composites were examined as individual outcomes in our secondary analyses. We also examined two unique outcomes in our secondary analyses: generalized development of children (GSED development) and child development (composite of PEDS:DM receptive and expressive language, PEDS:DM social-emotional skills, ASQ-3 communication, problem solving, and personal social skills, SDQ prosocial skills, SDQ internalizing and externalizing difficulties, and GSED development).

Use and engagement with BS-VT was operationalized as the number of books completed in BookSmart, the number of Vroom Tips TM completed, and as a dichotomous engagement variable: if a participant completed any books or Vroom Tips TM throughout the intervention, they were scored as "yes" for having engaged, otherwise participants were scored as "no". Notably, we removed outliers (n = 4, 1% of sample), defined as participants in the 99th percentile, for the number of completed books or Vroom Tips TM when examining our third research question. This method was used as standard inter-quartile outlier methods did not suit the zero-inflated data and to minimize the number of data points eliminated.

Composite scores were created following the method of Anderson (2008). Each component score is first standardized, then the composite is created from the weighted average of each component score. Weights are determined by the inverse of the covariance matrix of the standardized scores. Notably, for any participants who had missing scores for any given variable (i.e., they chose not to respond), their score was calculated using a covariance matrix that excluded this variable. If a participant only had one scored variable in the composite, they were excluded from the relevant analyses.

Models

Due to technical issues, some participants' child's age was calculated as 0 when completing their endline survey, causing them to not see most of the child measures (all but the PEDS:DM academic skill questions were hidden). As such, children with an endline age of 0 were excluded (n = 30, 6% of sample) from models examining child outcomes.

To account for multiple comparisons, we generated q values. Each research question had its own calculation for q values, creating three sets for main models (RQ1, RQ2, RQ3), and four sets for supplementary models (RQ1: secondary outcome main models; RQ1: all interaction models; RQ2: secondary outcome main models; RQ2: all interaction models).

Study 2 -Participant Recruitment

An initial screening process was conducted by MoyaApp to identify potential participants, as in study 1.100 users matching this criteria were sent a survey link through REDCap in which they needed to pass two additional screening checkpoints. Potential participants were first asked to select the age ranges of the children they care for. If they indicated that they have a child within the age range of 3-5 years old, they proceeded to the next form where they were informed about the study requirements and were asked whether they consent to participate. Those who consented proceeded to the pilot survey where they were first asked to provide birth dates for their child(ren) between 3 and 5 years old, to confirm that their children are in the target age range. Ineligible participants did not complete the remainder of the survey.

After receiving survey responses, the research team messaged participants via WhatsApp to schedule the semi-structured interviews. Participants completed a baseline interview between November 3 and November 14, 2025. Afterwards, they were prompted to use BS-VT for an intervention period of 3 weeks. During this time, they received 3 messages through MoyaApp's messaging system reminding them to use BS-VT. The interviewer also sent instructions to participants on how to access BookSmart. BS-VT usage and engagement were monitored during the 3-week intervention period. Participants were then messaged via WhatsApp to participate in the endline interview, which took place between November 25 and December 5, 2025. All interviews were conducted remotely through WhatsApp audio calls to ensure accessibility and low data usage. Interviews were recorded using Loom (Loom, n.d.) and transcribed using Fireflies.ai (Fireflies.ai, n.d.). Participants were compensated 105 rand for their time after completing the endline interview.

Study 2 -Interview Questions Baseline Questions:

1. During your day-to-day interactions with your child, what activities do you do to help them learn and develop? This could be activities that help a child focus, help them manage their emotions, work with others, solve problems, etc.

2. Do you read with your child? IF YES What kind of books, stories, or other things do you read or talk about together? How often do you read together? And for how long? How often do you want to read together? Why is that? What would help support you? IF NO Do you want to read with your child? IF YES How often do you want to read together? Why is that? What would help support you? 3. Do you feel confident helping your child develop and learn new things? Are there areas where you need support? What would you want this support to look like? 4. Do you ever use your phone or another device when reading with your child? Do you ever use your phone or another device to get ideas for connecting with your child and helping them learn social or emotional skills? How so? OR Why not? 5. How important is it to talk and read with your child every day for learning and developing new skills? Endline Questions: 1. I'm interested in how you and your child use the Booksmart app: How often do you read together using Booksmart? How often do you want to read together? Why is that? 8. Is there anything else you want to tell me about the app, the tips, or how you help your child learn and develop? IF TIME/IF NOT ALREADY DISCUSSED: Would you like to see any changes to the books or activities offered by the app? Are there any additional books or activities you would like? What about your child? Will you continue using it?

Study 2 -Data Analysis Baseline coding themes of interest included: caregiver-child learning activities, reading practices, reading aspirations, caregiver confidence, resources and barriers, technology use, perceived importance of reading, and child agency. Endline coding themes of interest included: BookSmart usage, BookSmart app perception, Vroom Tips TM usage, Vroom Tips TM perception, overall suggestions/confidence change/continue use, language, reminder, and motivation. Although we began coding with the a priori codes, in line with a combination deductive-inductive approach, we added additional codes as needed. These additional codes were developed inductively based on patterns that emerged from the interview data. Subsequently, codes and themes were refined throughout the analysis process. Tables S1 and S2 outline the final codes and themes.

Study 1 -Sample Characteristics

We found a significant difference between baseline shared reading time and 60 month old children's problem solving skills across treatment groups. However, upon being combined into their final constructs (i.e., parenting practices [p = .070] and cognitive skills [p = .549]), no significant differences were identified.

Children in the Sample With Disabilities or Disorders

Of the participants in the three treatment conditions, 8 (BookSmart Alone n = 2, Goal-Setting Messages n = 4, Reminder Messages n = 2) accessed BookSmart throughout the intervention. Additionally, of the participants who accessed BookSmart, only 2 (25%) completed a book or Vroom Tip TM within it. The small sample size (n = 19) limits any inferential statistical analyses. However, a two-sample proportion test was conducted to determine if there was a statistically significant difference in the proportion of participants who accessed between caregivers of children with disabilities (n₁ = 8, p̂₁ = .42) and caregivers of neurotypical children (n₂ = 312, p̂₂ = .52). The results were not statistically significant (2 = 0.389, p = 0.532) indicating that usage is similar between the two sub-samples. See Table S18.

The number of participants in each treatment group who accessed BookSmart at least once throughout the intervention period, regardless of whether they completed the endline survey. Note. Mean, standard deviation, range, and count were calculated using only data from participants who accessed the app throughout the intervention. Notably, despite our best attempts to block their access to the app, some participants in the control group (n = 48) still signed onto BookSmart throughout the intervention.

The most popular Vroom Tip TM type was tips for during snacktime, with 111 of these tips completed by participants through the intervention. Their popularity was followed by tips targeting early learning moments during playtime (n = 54), tips targeted towards expecting caregivers or those with very young children (i.e., less than 2 years old; n = 30), tips for when families were cleaning up (n = 23), and tips for when families were on the go (n = 23). Other tips completed included tips for when families were doing laundry (n = 20), tips for during mealtime (n = 19), tips for when families were getting dressed (n = 15), tips for during bedtime (n = 14), tips for during bathtime (n = 11), tips for "anytime, anywhere" (n = 8), tips for when families were at the park (n = 7), tips for when families were at appointments (n = 7), tips for when families were at the store (n = 6), and school readiness tips (n = 6). Note. Correlations exclude participants from the control group. Correlations between (A) baseline and (B) endline caregiver-level and child-level measures with engagement data. Insignificant values (p > .05) are left blank.

What would help support you? What books do you read? What books do you like the most? What books does your child like the most? How were you reading, looking at pictures? In English or in another language? Or a mix? How do you feel about the pictures? How does your child feel about the pictures? Does your child ever use the app without you? 2. How do you feel about the Booksmart app?

Why is that? OR What would make it better? How does your child feel about the app and the tips and activities? Do you prefer reading a hard copy or cellphone? Does your child ever ask to read more often, or the book again? Do you have a regular time for reading? Mealtime, bedtime, playtime? Do you find the activity of reading together enjoyable? Did your child ever ask to do the tips/activities again/often? Why is that? OR What would make them better? 3. You received Vroom Tips through the app that suggest activities for connecting with children to help them learn and develop important skills.

By skills, we mean things like learning to focus, work with others, or solve problems: How do you use the tips to connect with your child? How often do you use them? Which categories or types of tips and activities did you and your child like the most? Mealtime? Bedtime? Playtime? Etc. Did you do any activities like these before the app? If so, what did you do? 4. How easy or difficult was it to make Booksmart and Vroom Tips part of your day-to-day life? How easy or difficult were they to use? Why is that? OR What would make you use them more? Were there things you did not have at home (like a ball or paper) that made it hard to do the tips? If so, what things did you not have? 5. You might have received some messages from Moya App reminding you to use BookSmart and Vroom tips. Did you see them?

IF SO

How did you feel about the content of the messages? Did the wording make sense? Were the animations engaging? Did the messages encourage you to use BookSmart or try new learning activities with your child? Why or why not? Is there anything that could make the messages better or more motivating? 6. How confident do you feel about helping your child learn new things and develop?

Are there things that are hard for you when helping your child learn and develop? What kind of help would make it easier? Did the Booksmart app and Vroom Tips and activities make you feel more or less confident about supporting your child to learn and develop? 7. Do you think reading with Booksmart and doing the tip activities helps your child learn and develop? How important is that to you?
